_about: Ending narration and the 'What Dawnmere remembers' epilogue. Epilogue lines are shown when their ending matches (or is omitted) and their condition holds. Within a group, only the first matching line is shown, so put the most specific lines first.

keeper.title: THE KEEPER
lines: At sunrise, the villagers heard the bell once again.
And somewhere in the village, someone had forgotten a kindness they would never know to miss.

promise.title: THE UNBROKEN PROMISE
lines: For the first time in centuries, Dawnmere faced the darkness without a bell.
No one knew what the morning would bring.
But everyone remembered why they had chosen to see it.

chorus.title: THE CHORUS
lines: The bell rang one final time.
But to return what it could.
And that night, Dawnmere learned a different way to stand against the dark.

epilogue.text: You don't remember Orin. You keep an old chair by your window anyway, and you don't know why it makes you feel safe.
Orin's echo went quiet with the bell. You remember all of him, every flat note he ever sang.
When the bell rang the thirteenth time, the tower filled with a girl's laughter. Somewhere inside it, an old man was laughing too.
Mara woke humming. She didn't have the words yet. She sang it anyway, badly, down by the river, until her son came home to hear it.
Mara's lullaby came back to her the way a smell does: all at once, and from nowhere.
Mara knows where her song went now. She has started writing new ones. They are terrible. Her son loves them.
Mara still can't remember the lullaby. Some nights she stands at the forge door and listens to the bell for a long time.
Mara hung her lantern on the broken bell's pin by the forge door, and lit it every night until morning.
Pip taught the Gathering Song to anyone who would stand still long enough, and several people who wouldn't.
Pip still hums the old tune. These days, fewer people ask Pip to stop.
Pip kept humming. Somebody had to.
Brother Alden began a new record: every name in Dawnmere, written by everyone. It is very long and full of spelling mistakes. He has never been prouder of a book.
Tobin got Elsie back, the memory of her at least. He keeps the lamp by the well lit all night now. If she ever finds the road again, she'll know which light is his.
Tobin's lantern came back down the tower road still lit. He hung it on the post by the well, and on the longest nights he stands beside it, keeping the promise on purpose now.
Tobin still doesn't remember Elsie's face. But he knows her name now, and he says it every time he lights the lamp by the well.
Tobin still lights the lamp by the well twice a night. You never told him why. Some promises keep themselves.
Tobin stopped lighting the lantern by the well twice a night. Now he lights it once, and sits with it, and says her name.
Tobin still lights the lantern by the well twice a night. Some habits are the shape a memory leaves behind.
At dawn after the bell sang, someone walked out to the old crossing and lit the lantern on the post. The watchman wasn't there any more. He didn't need to be.
The lantern on the post by the old crossing is lit every evening now. Nobody remembers who started doing it.
The tower road was quiet after that night. Someone had chosen to remember a soldier with no name.
Travellers on the tower road say they feel watched. Kindly, the way a good guard watches.
The bell rang every sundown, twelve times, as it always had. Nobody asked what it cost. Only you knew they should have.
Every night, Dawnmere lit its lanterns and stood at its doors until the mist went home. Some nights were very long. Nobody faced them alone.
At dusk the whole village gathers in the square and sings thirteen notes. The bell rings once at the end, to say: we are still here.
